Meetings are broadcast live on Glendale TV, viewable on Spectrum Cable, channel 6, and AT&T U-
verse, channel 99. Meetings are also streamed live in high definition (HD) on the city's webpage,
glendaleca.gov/live, on YouTube.com/myglendale, and on Apple TV, Roku, and Amazon Fire
devices using a free app called Screenweave and choosing “Glendale TV” from the menu. Meetings
are also archived on the City Website for viewing anytime at glendaleca.gov/agendas. Call (818)
548-4013 for program schedules. DVDs of the proceedings are available for purchase in the City
Clerk's Office. For public comments and questions during the meeting, call (818) 937-8100. Public
comments on a specific agenda item will be taken when that agenda item is discussed. If you have
any question about matters on the agenda, or requests for assistance, please contact the City Clerk
at (818) 548-2090 during regular business hours.
  PLEASE TURN OFF CELLULAR PHONES WHILE INSIDE THE MEETING LOCATION
In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990, auxiliary hearing aids, sign
language translation, and Braille transcripts are available upon request. Assisted listening devices
are available same-day upon request. At least 48 hours (or two business days) notice is required for
requests regarding sign language translation and Braille transcription services. All documents
related to open session items on this agenda that are received less than 72 hours prior to this
meeting, and are public records, will be available for review in the Office of the City Clerk, 613 E.
Broadway, RM 110, Glendale, CA 91206.
Translation services are provided for meetings through the use of bilingual staff for speakers who
wish to utilize the service as available. Speakers should state their request by contacting the City
Clerk’s office at (818) 548-2090, at least 24 hours prior to the scheduled meeting. Please specify
the language for which you require translation. The exclusive use of City provided interpreters is not
required and persons are welcome to use their own interpreter or speak in their native language.

5. CITY COUNCIL/STAFF COMMENTS
  Mayor Kassakhian and his colleagues attended the League of California Cities Conference
  where discussions took place about new laws and the housing challenges that many cities
  face. He also attended the Independent Cities Association Annual Winter Conference where
  he heard a presentation by LA County Sheriff Luna. On January 25th, Kassakhian attended an
  event organized by the Armenian National Committee and LA for All where a discussion took
  place on Armenophobia. He stated that although Armenians have been classified as
  Caucasians, they have historically faced and continue to face discrimination and hate speech.
  He mentioned the recent incident during a demonstration protest on the streets of West Los
  Angeles in Beverly Hills where protesters came across posted flyers along their path that
  contained hate speech directed towards Armenians. He hoped that the City of Beverly Hills
  will properly address this incident and expressed his disappointment in the way in which this
  was classified by their police department as protected speech under the First Amendment
  rather than hate speech. Kassakhian asked the City to reach out to the County Supervisor’s
  Office and departments in Los Angeles to discuss how to enlighten and educate people so
  these acts of hate, whether targeting the Armenian Community or any other community, are
  not tolerated.

  Councilmember Najarian spoke to the Vice-Mayor of the City of Beverly Hills and expressed
  his disappointment regarding the acts of hate that occurred during the protest. Unfortunately,
  the vice-mayor stated that although the flyers were hateful, they were protected under the First
  Amendment. Najarian stated that the City of Beverly Hills did put out a statement, but it was
  not a strong one. He explained that the City of Beverly Hill’s response was especially
  disappointing given that their current City Manager was a former City of Glendale department
  head and should have had a clear understanding of what a threat of genocide means to
  Armenians. Najarian indicated that perhaps Glendale City Council should send a letter to the
  Mayor and City Manager of Beverly Hills asking them to put out stronger statements
  condemning these acts.

  Councilmember Asatryan joined her colleagues in condemning the acts that took place in
  Beverly Hills. She stated that the statement released by the Beverly Hills Police Department
  was inadequate and unacceptable, and that it behooves all leaders to take a strong stance on
  acts of hate, regardless of whether or not they believe that something is classified as freedom
  of speech. Asatryan drafted a letter but has not had a chance to send it to the City of Beverly
  Hills. She joins her colleagues in the call for Glendale City Council to demand more from the
  City of Beverly Hills. She noted that there was another incident where the City Manager of
  Beverly Hills inappropriately categorized events impacting the Armenian Community and had
  to apologize after Councilmember Asatryan pointed her error.

  2
   Kassakhian went to an event hosted by the Homenetmen Ararat Chapter where there was a
  screening of a documentary called “What will become of us.” It was about the Armenian
  community and how it has coped with the trauma of the genocide. The documentary was
  made by an Armenian-American filmmaker and a Jewish filmmaker. Kassakhian asked the
  Jewish filmmaker why he directed this documentary about Armenians. The director responded
  by talking about the commonalities between the Jewish and Armenian experience and how
  justice denied to one community impacts all communities. Kassakhian talked about the need
  for people to speak out and remind others of the history of these atrocities so that they don’t
  repeat. He also added that speaking up is important so that people who commit acts of hate,
  such as the ones in Beverly Hills, are not emboldened by our silence.

  Councilmember Devine expressed her regrets regarding the events that took place in the City
  of Beverly Hills and stated that these acts of hatred were unacceptable, and she hoped that
  the City of Glendale can speak up about it. She nominated Roland Kedikian for the Glendale
  Water and Power Commission. Devine commended and thanked Senator Portantino for
  holding a town hall meeting on gun violence, safety, and trauma, in the wake of the mass
  shooting that happened in the City of Monterey Park. She stated that what she learned from
  this townhall was that there are currently 400,000 firearms in the U.S. and the most dangerous
  aspect of mass violence is the accessibility of guns at home. She also talked about the
  importance of storing and locking up firearms in a safe place. Devine mentioned that it is
  important to report suspicious activities and for law enforcement to identify individuals who
  should not own guns. She asked the public to call #988 if they knew anyone who was in a
  mental crisis. Devine, Police Chief Sid, and Mayor Kassakhian attended an event where six
  young women became the inaugural class of female eagle scouts for the Homenetmen Ararat
  Chapter.

  Councilmember Brotman echoed the comments made by other councilmembers regarding the
  incident in Beverly Hills and was disturbed to hear that there was not a strong response by the
  City of Beverly Hills. He indicated that he will join his colleagues on the council in sending a
  letter to the City of Beverly Hills to demand a stronger response. Brotman received a letter
  asking why the city does not have a turf rebate program. He stated the city does have one and
  asked staff to feature it prominently on the website to get the message out to the public.
  Brotman mentioned that the City of Los Angeles’ turf rebate program increased to $5.00 per
  square foot while the City of Glendale’s is $2.00 per square foot. He asked staff to provide a
  memo on the effectiveness of increasing the rebate amount in Glendale’s turf rebate program.
  Brotman attended the Independent Cities Association meeting and learned about PFAS (a
  class of chemicals that are used in fire-fighting foams and food ware that can have lasting
  consequences on our health). According to the meeting, these chemicals can be found in
  the water supply of cities that have the following: water utilities, wastewater treatment plant,
  landfill, and airport. He asked staff to learn more about the impacts of PFAS on our water
  supply and what our city can do to help alleviate these conditions that impact our water
  supply.
